Vocal Music. Music created with and for the human voice as the primary instrument, encompassing opera, art songs, madrigals, spirituals, pop vocals, and all sung music. The voice is unique among instruments in that it can simultaneously produce melody, text, and emotional expression through language, making vocal music a synthesis of music and word. Vocal music has remained the most universal and accessible form of music-making across all cultures and historical periods, from solo singing to large choral works.

Vocal music is distinct from instrumental music by its use of the human voice as the primary sound-producing instrument. Four primary voice classifications—soprano, alto, tenor, bass—divide the vocal range into functional categories, with additional subdivisions like mezzo-soprano and baritone for greater specificity.

Opera synthesizes vocal performance with drama, orchestral accompaniment, and stagecraft, making it one of history's most elaborate vocal music genres. Madrigals, Renaissance polyphonic songs, showcased sophisticated word-painting, where musical figures reflected textual meaning. The art song, or lied, paired solo voice with piano, creating intimate settings for poetry by composers like Franz Schubert. Choir and choral music, from Renaissance motets to modern chorales, demonstrated how voices blend in harmony across multiple parts.

Folk and vernacular singing traditions—spirituals, work songs, ballads—preceded and persist alongside composed classical vocal music. Vocal technique training includes breath support, resonance control, diction, and interpretation; classical singers typically study for years to develop proper technique and prevent vocal strain. Popular and rock singing, while distinct from classical vocal training, still requires significant technical skill to project, control pitch, and sustain performances night after night.

Vocal music carries text alongside melody, creating unique expressive possibilities unavailable to instrumental music; lyrics can reinforce, contradict, or layer meanings onto the musical line. Vocal harmony, with multiple singers at different pitches, creates rich timbral blending; barbershop, close harmonies, and choral blend are prized for their consonance and warmth. The voice ages and changes throughout life; vocal pedagogy addresses the child voice, adolescent voice change, adult voice development, and aging voices differently. Contemporary vocal music spans genres from classical opera to hip-hop to electronic vocal processing; the human voice remains central to music-making across all cultures and styles.
